claims.claim: Supporters point to annual independent audits, annual online district accounting, and a ban on administrative spending as safeguards for the school funds.

Protects schools and health care from cuts, including teacher layoffs and lost access to care or Medi-Cal.
Protects local classroom funding through restrictions on administrative spending, independent audits, public accounting, and penalties for misuse.
Maintaining education funding also protects funding for firefighters, emergency response, and wildfire protection.
Revenue supports Rainy Day Fund investments that protect schools and health care during economic downturns.

points_against.point: Making the higher rates permanent breaks the promise that the tax increases would be temporary.
Permanent higher taxes worsen California's already high cost of living.
The state should address waste, fraud, overspending, and budget mismanagement rather than make higher taxes permanent.
Large spending increases have not delivered promised improvements in schools, infrastructure, or public safety.

who_is_affected: High-income California taxpayers who pay the higher rates

claims.claim: The Legislative Analyst estimates the measure would raise state and local government costs by tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year; the exact cost depends on future choices.
The measure keeps vote-by-mail voting and requires the state to provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one.
Supporters argue that voter ID can increase participation because voters who trust elections are more likely to take part.

Supporters say signature mismatches can lead to rejected mail ballots and extra steps for voters; they cite their argument that more than 100,000 ballots were rejected for mismatches and more than 200,000 voters faced hassles in the last election.
claims.note: Both numbers appear in the supporters’ argument; the card appropriately attributes them rather than treating them as analyst findings.

claims.claim: Supporters expect regular independent audits to give the public more confidence in how election officials follow the new rules.
The measure requires in-person voters to show government-issued ID and mail voters to designate an ID in their registration and provide matching ID-number digits on their ballot envelope.
Opponents warn that putting ID-number information on mail ballot envelopes could expose voters to identity theft and force a choice between privacy and voting.

Opponents worry that getting ID could require transportation, time off work, childcare, or obtaining required documents. They say seniors, students, low-income workers, voters of color, and women who changed their names at marriage may face the greatest burdens.

Opponents warn that an ID-number mismatch, an outdated address, or a misspelled name on ID could put a valid vote at risk; they also say a voter who does not designate an ID might not receive a mail ballot.
claims.note: These warnings are stated in the official opposition argument; they are not all independently established by the analyst.

claims.claim: California already requires U.S. citizenship to vote in state and federal elections and most local elections; the analyst says voters establish identity during registration and mail-ballot signatures are checked before ballots are counted.
About 13 million people voted by mail and about 3 million voted in person in California’s November 2024 election.
The measure requires voters to provide added identifying information each time they cast a ballot, with different requirements for in-person and mail voting.
The Legislative Analyst estimates added costs would likely exceed any savings from fewer people being registered to vote.

points_for.point: Voter ID would increase election trust and participation rather than suppress turnout.
Voting would remain accessible through continued mail voting and other conveniences, with free voter ID available.
Current mail-ballot signature matching puts votes at risk and creates substantial voter hassles.
Citizenship verification, accurate voter lists, and independent audits would improve election management and accountability.
The measure is a broadly supported bipartisan California solution, not a project about Trump or national partisan control.

points_against.point: The measure is part of a Trump-aligned, billionaire-funded effort to suppress voters and consolidate partisan power.
The measure would waste substantial recurring taxpayer funds pursuing election conspiracy claims.
Putting personal identifying information on mail-ballot envelopes creates identity-theft and privacy risks.
New ID-designation and matching requirements could prevent eligible voters from receiving mail ballots or having their votes counted.
Even free IDs entail transportation, time, childcare, and documentation burdens that disproportionately affect vulnerable groups and women with changed names.

card.official_title: PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
card.plain_title: Require government ID to vote in person or by mail
card.yes_means: Require voters to use government-issued ID to vote in person. Mail voters must designate a government-issued ID in their voter registration and put the last four digits of that designated number on their ballot envelope. If the digits do not match, the ballot is invalid. The measure also requires election officials to make best efforts to verify voter citizenship, report yearly on verification, provide free voter ID cards on request, and undergo regular audits. The Legislature would pass laws to fill in details.
card.no_means: Keep the current system: voters generally identify themselves by signing in person or signing a mail-ballot envelope, and election officials verify mail-ballot signatures. No new ID-number requirements, citizenship-verification reports, voter ID card program, or audits under this measure would take effect.
who_is_affected: People who vote in person, who would need to present government-issued ID
People who vote by mail, who would need to designate an ID and provide matching ID-number information
County and state election officials, who would verify identities and citizenship and carry out reporting and audits
Voters who request a free state-issued voter ID card
